General Information  
Purpose of this document:  
These notes were developed to help teachers understand the depth and breadth of the standards. 
In some cases, information provided in this document goes beyond the scope of the standard and 
can be used for background and enrichment information. Please remember that the goal of science 
teaching is to have students engage with the content by incorporating all 3 dimensions of science 
into each lesson. Also, teachers should utilize phenomena to provide students with real-world 
problems that can be figured out and eventually explained, argued, modeled, or investigated. (Note: 
The standards provide the minimum expectation of student learning outcomes and performances. 
This document is intended to provide background information for teachers and parents.) 
 
Within this document you will find the following information: 
1. Background information for the 3-dimensions of science teaching: 
a. Science and engineering practices (SEPs) are the activities that scientists do as part of 
their work. Teachers need students to engage in the work just as scientists would. This 
means that teachers need to engage students in science, and they do that by 
incorporating the science and engineering practices into each lesson that students 
engage with. This involves students in the work of scientists and allows students to 
build knowledge while gaining an understanding of the purpose of science.  
b. Crosscutting concepts (CCCs) are the concepts that span all science disciplines and 
classes. The CCCs can function as lenses that students use to view phenomena, 
scaffolding to build new knowledge around, and a way to activate prior knowledge.  
c. Disciplinary core ideas (DCIs) are the things that have been considered content in the 
past. These core ideas are addressed throughout a student’s K-12 school career and 
build in complexity as students continually encounter each core idea. 
2. Phenomena examples 
3. Initial student ideas- All students come into classes with prior knowledge that act as building 
blocks for students to build their knowledge on. Sometimes this prior knowledge is an 
inaccurate representation of the world around them and, in the past, this has been called a 
misconception. However, we now know, that these misconceptions are just a facet of student 
learning that still work as building blocks and need to be approached as something to build 
from rather than replace. So, in the future we will refer to this as a facet of student learning 
and the ideas as potential initial student ideas.

Teacher notes  
2nd Grade Standards 
Earth and Space Science  
Earth and space sciences investigate processes that operate on Earth and address its place in the 
solar system and in the galaxy. The 2nd grade unit this will cover is based on patterns in the day and 
in the night. In 2nd grade Earth science students will gain an understanding that Sunlight warms the 
Earth’s surface, the Sun, Moon, and stars and their apparent motion in the day and night sky have 
patterns, and some events on Earth occur in cycles, like day and night.  
S2E1. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about stars having 
different sizes and brightness. 
 
Background:  
The science and engineering practice in the standard, obtain, evaluate, and communicate, is 
addressed throughout the GSE.  This is the overarching science and engineering practice for each of 
the standards across K-12.  The goal of this science and engineering practice is for students to obtain 
information (gather information from different sources and experiences), evaluate information (reason 
with it, organize it), and then communicate information (share through another practice such as 
through a model, by constructing an argument, etc.). Each of the GSE elements has additional 
science and engineering practices which students should engage in.   
Stars that are farther away appear smaller and dimmer.  Because the Sun is so much closer than 
other stars, it looks much bigger and brighter. Objects that are closer to you seem larger than objects 
that are farther away. 
Students should obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about stars having different sizes 
and brightness through the use of videos, images, and observations. Images that are streaming from 
the recently launched James Webb telescope can provide opportunities for obtaining information and 
asking questions.

S2E1. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about stars having 
different sizes and brightness.  
a. Ask questions to describe the physical attributes (size and brightness) of stars.  
 
Background:  
Stars are huge balls of burning gases that make their own light and heat energy. Most stars are made 
of two gases called hydrogen and helium. Hydrogen is the lightest element (gas) on the Periodic 
Table of the Elements. As the hydrogen gas in a star is squeezed due to gravity, it produces huge 
amounts of energy, which makes it glow. Under heat and pressure, hydrogen elements can fuse 
together to form another gas, Helium, through a process called nuclear fusion. The size, temperature, 
brightness, and color of stars vary. The color of a star is determined by its temperature. 
 
Stars that are farther away appear smaller and dimmer.  Because the Sun is so much closer than 
other stars, it looks much bigger and brighter. Objects that are closer to you seem larger than objects 
that are farther away.  
Specific Types of Stars (for teacher education purposes - not required to be taught in 2nd grade): 
There are many different types of stars. Stars that are in their main sequence (normal stars) are 
categorized by their color. The smallest stars are red and don't give off much of a glow. Medium size 
stars are yellow, like the Sun. The largest stars are blue and are very bright. The larger the main 
sequence star, the hotter and brighter they are. During the life cycle of a star, stars are born in 
nebulae (areas with hydrogen gas). Hydrogen fuses together to form helium. Helium fuses together to 
form other gases. As this process takes place, stars grow larger and brighter. 
● Dwarfs - Smaller stars are called dwarf stars. Red and yellow stars are generally called dwarfs. 
A brown dwarf is one that never quite got large enough for nuclear fusion to occur. A white 
dwarf is the remnants of the collapse of a red giant star. 
● Giants - Giant stars may be main sequence stars like a blue giant, or stars that are expanding 
like red giants. Some supergiant stars are as big as the entire Solar System!

● Neutrons - A neutron star is created from the collapse of a giant star. It's very tiny, but very 
dense. 
Students should be encouraged to ask questions and to describe the physical attributes (size and 
brightness) of stars. NASA has several websites dedicated to stars and space, including NASA 
Space Place. 
 
Potential initial student ideas: 
• The Sun is larger and brighter than other stars. 
• The Sun is not a star. 
• Stars are just light, and they do not have other properties.  
 
Science and Engineering Practice:  
The science and engineering practice in this element is to ask questions to describe the size and 
brightness of stars. After students look at images of stars, they should ask questions. A good strategy 
to use is “what do you notice” followed by “what do you wonder.” Generating questions, especially 
investigable questions, is an important practice of scientists. 
The teacher can display an image of various stars and allow students to make observations. Then 
have students ask questions about the stars. This could be done with a see, think, wonder chart.  
Crosscutting Concept: patterns; scale, proportion, and quantity 
Phenomenon examples:  
• Is the Sun the largest brightest star? 
• What things help identify stars? 
 
S2E1. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about stars having 
different sizes and brightness. 
b. Construct an argument to support the claim that although the Sun appears to be 
the brightest and largest star, it is actually medium in size and brightness. 
 
Background:  
Stars that are farther away appear smaller and dimmer.  Because the Sun is so much closer than 
other stars, it looks much bigger and brighter. Objects that are closer to you seem larger than objects 
that are farther away. 
The Sun is a medium sized star. It appears to be the largest because of scale: it is the closest star to 
Earth. There are actually stars much bigger than our Sun but because they are so far away, they 
appear to be smaller.

Students should be gaining information about stars and the different sizes and brightness of the 
different stars in the sky. They will use this information to construct arguments about the fact that the 
Sun looks the brightest and the largest, however, it is actually not the largest star in the sky.  
Potential initial student ideas: 
• The Sun is the brightest and/or largest star. 
• The Sun is not a star.  
 
Science and Engineering Practice:  
The science and engineering practice in this element is construct an argument to support the claim 
that the Sun appears to be the brightest and largest star, but it is actually only a medium sized star. 
Students should use evidence from obtaining, evaluating and communicating information to support 
the claim. 
Constructing and using models may help students visualize how distance can affect the way objects 
appear. Students can stand different distances from a wall and shine different sized flashlights 
towards the wall. Flashlights that are closer to the wall will appear brighter than those shined from a 
further distance. This model can be used to help explain why stars that are a further distance appear 
smaller and dimmer. Caution students to not shine flashlights in each other’s eyes. Students can use 
data collected from this model to make their claims and construct their arguments. It is recommended 
that students collect their data first, then make a claim, and use the data from the investigation to 
construct their argument about how the Sun appears brighter than other stars in the sky even though 
it is only a medium sized star. 
Crosscutting concept: patterns; scale, proportion, and quantity 
Phenomenon examples:  
• Is the Sun the largest and brightest star? 
• What is the largest star?

understanding of the patterns of the Sun and the Moon and the Sun’s effect on

S2E2. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information to develop an 
understanding of the patterns of the Sun and the Moon and the Sun’s effect on 
Earth. 
a. Plan and carry out an investigation to determine the effect of the position of the 
Sun in relation to a fixed object on Earth at various times of the day. 
 
Background:  
While it appears that the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, the Sun really isn’t moving. It’s the 
Earth that is moving. It takes approximately 24 hours (1 day) to spin (rotate) one time.   
During the daytime, Sunlight only shines on the part of the Earth that is facing the Sun. The other side 
of the Earth has nighttime because it is dark (it’s facing away from the Sun). 
As Earth rotates, the part that was light turns away from the Sun and gets dark. The part that was 
dark moves towards the light. This pattern will repeat every 24 hours.  
Potential initial student ideas: 
• The Sun, Moon and stars are moving, and Earth is stationary.  
 
Georgia Department of Education

Science and Engineering Practice:  
The science and engineering practice in this element is to plan and carry out an investigation. 
Students should be given the opportunity to plan and investigate the effect of the position of the Sun 
in relation to a fixed object on Earth at various times of the day.  One way to do this is to investigate 
using a flashlight and small rubber ball globes. A sticky note or pushpin can be placed on a specific 
location and students can determine when it is dark and when it is light as the Earth rotates. Let 
students explore ways to model this phenomenon and construct an explanation about why we have 
day and night. 
Crosscutting concepts: patterns; cause and effect 
Phenomenon examples:  
• How do shadows move during the day? 
S2E2. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information to develop an 
understanding of the patterns of the Sun and the Moon and the Sun’s effect on 
Earth. 
b. Design and build a structure that demonstrates how shadows change throughout 
the day. 
 
Background:  
The science and engineering practice in this element is to design and build a structure to show how 
shadows change.  
When light cannot pass through an object, it creates a shadow. 
The Sun looks like it’s moving, but really, it’s just the Earth rotating. Because the Earth is rotating, the 
Sun’s light shines on objects from different directions as the day goes on. This causes the sizes and 
shapes of shadows to change.  
Your shadow is longest in the early morning and in the late afternoon. The Sun makes the longest 
shadows at the beginning and at the end of the day because at that time, the Sun is lowest in the sky 
and aimed at the sides of the various things on the Earth.  
 
When the Sun is directly above you, (around noon), there is little or no shadow because the light from 
the Sun is falling upon you from all the sides and there is hardly any dark region. 
 
Potential initial student ideas: 
• Shadows change on their own.  
• Shadow shape and size has nothing to do with the Sun position.  
 
 
Science and Engineering Practice:

The students should investigate how shadows change throughout the day and night (a flashlight can 
be used for this) and then design and build a structure to demonstrate their understanding of how 
shadows are created and changed throughout the day. The flashlight can be used to model the Sun 
at different positions shining on an object like a paper doll on a popsicle stick.

S2E2. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information to develop an 
understanding of the patterns of the Sun and the Moon and the Sun’s effect on 
Earth. 
c. Represent data in tables and/or graphs of the length of the day and night to 
recognize the change in seasons. 
Background: 
As the Earth moves around the Sun during a year, the tilt of the Earth determines how long our days 
and nights are.  The northern half of the Earth where we live in Georgia is tilted towards the Sun in 
the summer, making daytime longer than night. In winter, this reverses. The northern half of the Earth 
tilts away from the Sun and nighttime becomes longer. 
The tilt of the Earth on its axis, also, determines the seasons. The United States and the Northern 
Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in July (summer) and tilted away from the Sun in January 
(winter). The tilt leads to longer days and longer access to the Sun’s heat and is the reason we 
experience summer and the opposite in winter. Teachers note: The tilt of Earth’s axis addressed in 
later grades. 
Potential initial student ideas: 
• Many people believe that the seasons are based on distance to the Sun. 
Science and Engineering Practice:  
The science and engineering practice in this element is to represent data in a table or chart to show 
how the length of day changes with the seasons.   
Students should keep a data table throughout the year to record the length of the day and night in 
relation to the seasons.  (This could be done as a class by displaying a table on the board and 
recording the information together each day.)  A grade level appropriate graph could be used to show 
how the length of day changes throughout the school year from summer to fall to winter to spring. 
Data could be collected once daily or once per week. 
Crosscutting Concept: patterns

S2E2. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information to develop an 
understanding of the patterns of the Sun and the Moon and the Sun’s effect on 
Earth. 
d. Use data from personal observations to describe, illustrate, and predict how the 
appearance of the Moon changes over time in a pattern. (Clarification statement: 
Students are not required to know the names of the phases of the Moon or 
understand the tilt of the Earth.)  
Background:  
The Moon doesn’t give off light itself, the Moonlight we see is actually the Sun’s light reflected off the 
surface of the Moon. 
Remember, there is a lot of movement taking place (Earth and the Moon rotate on their axis or spin 
around). The Moon revolves or orbits around the Earth and the Earth revolves or orbits around the 
Sun. Remember from our day and night flashlight model, day and night is caused by the Earth’s 
spinning around its axis and different parts of the Earth facing the Sun at different times during the 
day.  
As the Moon revolves around (orbits) the Earth, the Sun lights up different parts of the Moon, making 
it seem as if the Moon is changing shape. In actual fact, it’s just our view of it that’s changing. 
Depending on where the Moon is in relation to Earth, it may appear to be a different size or different 
shape. Having students keep a monthly Moon journal can help them see the patterns of changes that 
happen in the shape of the Moon over time. Students should keep records of the changes and draw 
what they see in the sky each night (with an adult’s help) or from data available online. The teacher 
should keep a record of these changes on a calendar for the students to use as well.  
As days pass, the part of the Moon we see appears to change shape. More of the Moon becomes 
visible. Be cautious about saying it gets bigger but note that more of the Moon becomes visible and 
as time goes by less of the Moon is visible. There is a phase that we see the whole Moon – this is a 
Full Moon and there is a phase that we see none of the Moon – this is the New Moon phase. Keeping 
a record of the phases for a month or more can help students see the repeating pattern. You can also 
show the students monthly and yearly Moon phase patterns. Students could check their birthday on a 
calendar to see what phase the Moon will be in on their birthday in an upcoming year. 
 
Teacher background knowledge.  This is not required of the students.:   
When more of the Moon is visible, (shape is getting bigger), it’s called ‘waxing’ and when it looks like 
it’s getting smaller, it’s ‘waning’. Once the face of the Moon is fully turned towards the Sun, it’s a Full 
Moon, and we see it all. But, as the Moon moves around the Earth, the face pointing towards us

gradually becomes hidden from the Sun until we can hardly see it at all – this is a New Moon. This 
terminology is addressed in later grade levels. 
 
Potential initial student ideas: 
• The moon has its own light source.  
• The moon shape is changing.  
 
Science and Engineering Practice:  
The science and engineering practice in this element is to use data from personal observations to 
describe, illustrate, and predict how the Moon changes over time.   
This element focuses on noticing the pattern and students should “use data from personal 
observations to describe, illustrate, and predict how the appearance of the Moon changes over time 
in a pattern. (Clarification statement: Students are not required to know the names of the phases of 
the Moon or understand the tilt of the Earth.) Patterns is an important crosscutting concepts used 
across all sciences. 
In this element, the students will use data from personal observations to describe, illustrate, and 
predict how the appearance of the Moon changes over time in a pattern.  This can be done in a 
science journal in which students predict what the Moon will look like each night and then draw the 
Moon each night for a given period of time.  Monthly and yearly Moon calendars which can be found 
online can help students see the regular repeating patterns on the Moon phase which is addressed 
more deeply in the 4th grade standards. 
 
Crosscutting Concept: patterns 
Phenomenon examples:  
• Moon observation  
 
 
 
 
 
 
S2E3. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about how weather, 
plants, animals, and humans cause changes to the environment. (Clarification 
statement: Changes should be easily observable and could be seen on school 
grounds or at home.)

Background:  
The science and engineering practice in the standard, obtain, evaluate, and communicate, is 
addressed throughout the GSE.  This is the overarching science and engineering practice for each of 
the standards across K-12.  The goal of this science and engineering practice is for students to obtain 
information (gather information from different sources and experiences), evaluate information (reason 
with it, organize it), and then communicate information (share through another practice such as 
through a model, by constructing an argument, etc.). Each of the GSE elements has additional 
science and engineering practices which students should engage in.   
In this unit, students will explore how weather, plants, animals and humans cause changes to the 
environment and the positive and negative consequences of those modifications. Students will 
interact with these influences using specific examples from the local community to construct an 
explanation of the cause-and-effect relationship that exists between the environment and these 
influences. 
Our environment is constantly changing in observable ways. The environment can be changed by the 
weather (wind, rain, seasonal changes, etc.), plants (new plant growth, invasive plants, etc.), animals 
(feeding on plants/other animals, waste, etc.) as well as humans. 
Consider the following vocabulary terms that students should encounter as they build core 
idea understanding. Vocabulary should be taught in context with new terms encountered by 
students as they work to figure out a phenomenon. This list may not be all inclusive of the 
terms that students could learn associated with this standard. 
• Environment  
• Change  
• Habitat  
• Animal  
• Plant  
• Weather  
• Drought  
• Erosion  
• Flood  
• Lightning  
 
 
S2E3. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about how weather, 
plants, animals, and humans cause changes to the environment. (Clarification 
statement: Changes should be easily observable and could be seen on school 
grounds or at home.)  
a. Ask questions to obtain information about major changes to the environment in 
your community. 
 
 
Georgia Department of Education

9.17.2022 Page 12 of 24 
 
Background:  
Major changes to the environment can occur in many ways. Weather events such as tornadoes, 
hurricanes, lightning strikes, drought, rain and many other weather events can lead to changes in any 
environment. Plants and animals can lead to changes in environments if their populations become too 
large or if they are in areas where they do not belong (invasive species). Humans, also, cause 
changes to the environment by building things, tearing things down, deforestation, pollution and in 
many other ways. All these different causes can affect the stability of a particular ecosystem such as 
the one surrounding your school. Students should be looking for changes to the environment and 
asking questions about what causes the changes, what kinds of changes there are and how to 
minimize the effects of the changes. 
Potential initial student ideas: 
• Environments change without cause.  
• Changes to the environment are always positive or negative.  
Science and Engineering Practice:  
The science and engineering practice for this element is to ask questions to obtain information about 
changes to the environment near where we live.  
One way this element may be addressed is by going on a science scavenger hunt in the school yard 
and allowing students the opportunity to obtain information to answer the following questions: 
Questions: 
● How has the weather changed our neighborhood, town or school grounds?   
● How have plants changed our neighborhood, town or school grounds?   
● How have animals changed our neighborhood, town or school grounds?   
● How have humans changed our neighborhood, town, or school grounds?  
Crosscutting Concept: cause and effect, energy and matter, stability and change, patterns 
Phenomenon examples:  
• Building a new building, park, playground, parking area, etc. around your school or 
neighborhood. 
• Kudzu  
• Drought  
S2E3. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about how weather, 
plants, animals, and humans cause changes to the environment. (Clarification 
statement: Changes should be easily observable and could be seen on school 
grounds or at home.)  
b. Construct an explanation of the causes and effects of a change to the environment 
in your community.  
 
Background:  
 
Georgia Department of Education 
THIS WORK IS LICENSED UNDER A CREATIVE COMMONS ATTRIBUTION -  NONCOMMERCIAL - SHAREALIKE 4.0 INTERNATIONAL LICENSE

Every change in the environment has a cause. The change itself is the effect. So, an example of this 
is the sides of a riverbank getting wider is caused by the movement of water in the river and running 
down the side when it rains. This water movement causes erosion of the land on the edges of the 
river. This is true of any change.  
Potential initial student ideas: 
• Not all changes in the environment have a cause. 
• The cause of a particular change may be different from what is actually causing the change.  
Science and Engineering Practice:  
The science and engineering practice in this element is to construct an explanation.  
Using the information students gathered in this last element, the students should construct an 
explanation of the causes and effects of changes to the environment in our community. See the 
questions below and examples of explanations of cause and effect in parenthesis:  
● How has the weather changed our neighborhood, town or school grounds)?  (Examples: 
Sun faded the plastic climbing structures on the playground, rain made holes in the 
ground, erosion, etc.)  
● How have plants changed our neighborhood, town or school grounds?  (Examples: 
roots of the tree broke the sidewalk, tree limb fell on the fence, pinecones on ground)  
● How have animals changed our neighborhood, town or school grounds?  (Examples: 
dog dug a hole, woodpecker made holes in the tree, dog used restroom in the yard, 
squirrels dropped acorns) 
● How have humans changed our neighborhood, town, or school grounds?  (Examples: 
grass has been knocked down/killed from students running on it, tree was cut down for 
building, land was dug up for new construction, people have littered, people have 
planted flowers) 
For each of the above questions, students should explain the cause of the change and the effects it 
has on the world around them.   
 
 
Crosscutting Concept: cause and effect 
Phenomenon examples:  
• Fading playground equipment  
• Erosion near the school  
• Building something near the school

Physical Science in 2nd grade covers force, motion, matter and how matter changes. The force and 
motion section asks students to examine pushes and pulls and how the size of an object impacts 
force and motion. When students examine matter, they are going to be looking into the structure of 
matter, properties of matter, and how heating or cooling can change the properties of matter. 
 
S2P1. Obtain, evaluate, and communicate information about the properties of 
matter and changes that occur in objects. 
Background:  
The science and engineering practice in the standard, obtain, evaluate, and communicate, is 
addressed throughout the GSE.  This is the overarching science and engineering practice for each of 
the standards across K-12.  The goal of this science and engineering practice is for students to obtain 
information (gather information from different sources and experiences), evaluate information (reason 
with it, organize it), and then communicate information (share through another practice such as 
through a model, by constructing an argument, etc.). Each of the GSE elements has additional 
science and engineering practices which students should engage in.   
In this unit, students classify matter according to physical properties.  They will conduct simple 
investigations to understand that when a structure is assembled and disassembled, the weight is the 
same as the weight of its parts. They will also explain how some changes are reversible and some 
are irreversible. This standard provides a foundation for the 5th grade standards of physical and 
chemical changes. When matter combines in a chemical change, it is similar to the rearrangement of 
the cubes or blocks modeled in the standard. In second grade, students get a foundation of some of 
the basic properties of matter. It isn’t necessary to use the same vocabulary as 5th, physical and 
chemical. Reversible and irreversible change provides important background for later grade levels.

something.   The shade a person sees.

i. Flexibility- the ability to bend without breaking

Background:  
Matter can change. Some changes can be reversed, and some changes are irreversible. Changes in 
matter can be changes in state or changes in the composition. An example of a change of state that 
can be reversed is freezing water because it can be changed back into liquid water. An example of an 
irreversible change is frying an egg because it is impossible to get the egg back into its uncooked 
state.  
Potential initial student ideas:

Reversible Change ‐ a change that can be turned back (example heating, freezing, and melting of 
water)  
Substance ‐ something made from only one material, such as water or copper    
Heat ‐ the type of energy that leads to a change of state (may make things feel warm)     
Melting ‐ to change from a solid to a liquid

c. Construct an explanation of an animal’s role in dispersing seeds or in the

Background:  
There are several types of seed dispersal. However, in 2nd grade, the required focus is primarily on 
the animal’s role in the spreading of the seeds. Here are examples of ways seeds can be spread from 
place to place:  
● Water (example in runoff, streams, or rivers)  
● Animals and Birds (they eat them and then release in their waste, they bury them, or they get 
stuck in their feathers or fur).  
● Gravity (they fall to the ground and roll down hills) 
● Explosions 
Pollination is a very important part of the life cycle of plants. A pollinator, such as a bee, hummingbird, 
butterfly, or bat, takes pollen between flowering plants.  They do this by moving pollen from plant to 
plant. This pollen then fertilizes the plant which means the plants can make seeds and reproduce (to 
make more plants)
